column1: # policy/ops/ops-sandbox.tsv — THE OPERATOR'S PER-TOOL SANDBOX TABLE (S2).
# THE AUTHOR IS THE OPERATOR, exactly like ops-aliases.tsv and ops-hosts.tsv.
# This table lets the operator TIGHTEN a host tool's sandbox below its
# compiled-in floor.  It is the palisade half of "configure the sandbox by
# policy": the proxy is the only process at the spawn, it already evaluates
# this operator policy in-process, and the pin (policy/ops/PINS) makes every
# edit a visible release — a per-generation Dhall spec would be invisible to
# the per-boot record, so datalog/ops policy owns the spec and Dhall has no
# role in v1 (do not re-open that decision).
# Columns (TAB-separated; '#' starts a comment):
#   tool        a HOST TOOL name (one of the proxy's pinned registry names —
#               host_time, host_cat, http_get).  An unknown tool is a STARTUP
#               REFUSAL naming the row.
#   promises    the tool's pledge tokens, space-separated, from the 23-token
#               cosmocc vocabulary (stdio rpath wpath cpath dpath flock fattr
#               inet unix dns tty recvfd proc exec id unveil sendfd settime
#               prot_exec vminfo tmppath chown anet).
#   landlock    "path:perms;path:perms;..." — the operator's ALLOWLIST of the
#               paths the tool may unveil beyond its static floor (the loader
#               + libc, which the spawn always adds).  perms is an unveil perm
#               string over {r,w,x,c}.
# SILENCE = THE FLOOR.  A tool with NO row here runs at its COMPILED-IN FLOOR
# — the LEAST it needs, measured from ldd — never "unsandboxed".  There is no
# unsandboxed state in the real build; the spawn ALWAYS wraps a floored tool
# in stage3.  This table's shipped state is the FLOOR for every tool (no
# rows), and the restriction a host tool actually faces is the compiled-in
# floor PLUS the operator's alias/host class tables (D3 + the totality check).
# DENY-MORE-ONLY, IN BOTH DIMENSIONS, ENFORCED AT THE SEAT (not just stated):
#   * promises — the row's tokens must be a SUBSET of the tool's floor tokens.
#     A token beyond the floor is a STARTUP REFUSAL naming the row and the
#     token (never a silent widening).  The row may also not drop `stdio` or
#     `exec` (the floor's own self-check: a floor without exec kills every
#     call, a floor without stdio breaks the program contract).
#   * landlock — the row's allowlist can only NARROW which paths the tool may
#     read: the spawn unveils EXACTLY the per-call judged path `:r` (and never
#     a path the call did not name), and only when that path appears in the
#     row's allowlist.  A path dropped from the row makes the call's open fail
#     EACCES while the alias table still judges the call allowed.  A perm wider
#     than the floor's per-call `r` is a STARTUP REFUSAL naming the row.
# RLIMITS ARE DELIBERATELY NOT HERE.  stage3's resource limits (RATTAN_RLIMITS)
# are a compiled-in floor field, not an operator lever: deny-more-only for
# rlimits is awkward and the operator has no business tuning them.
# ONE SPELLING.  The AUTHORITATIVE check of this table is the SEAT's own
# floor-subset composition (tools/fx-hostgate.c: ops_load_sandbox, run at
# startup, before the slave path is published).  policy/ops/eval_ops.py's
# --check-sandbox is GRAMMAR ONLY — the promise-token vocabulary, the landlock
# perm grammar, the tool-name charset — and it NEVER re-spells the registry:
# the registry (the floors) is the single source, so a floor edit and the
# python check can never drift into two different vocabularies.
# The table is pinned in policy/ops/PINS: editing it is a re-pin (a release),
# artifact + PINS in the SAME commit.
# The shipped state is the FLOOR (no rows).  To narrow host_cat to a specific
# readable set, add a row (the example below is commented out):
# host_cat
